It then tries all possible binary splits of the input string according to the structure of the start production (S → NT6 NT34), enumerating all possibilities for partitioning the string into substrings that could be generated by the right-hand side nonterminals.

For each attempt, the model details the possible productions, recursively explores splits based on the shape of the grammar, and at each step explicitly checks terminal and nonterminal possibilities by referencing the productions (e.g., "NT34 only generates terminals, so can't produce more than 1 token substring", etc).

The model further attempts to simulate the construction of a CYK parse table, listing for each terminal position which nonterminals can generate the single token, and then tries to reason about length-2 substrings, seeking possible binary productions that might expand bottom up to the start symbol.

At each stage, the model provides explicit references to the grammar's production rules, demonstrates unsuccessful attempts to construct a derivation, and repeatedly justifies why the derivation cannot proceed. It ultimately concludes, after systematic elimination of all possible derivation pathways, that the string cannot possibly be generated from the start symbol.

No guesswork or probabilities are involved—the approach is explicitly and rigorously deductive, attempting to build a full derivation tree or to show that none exists. This is the hallmark of the rule-based strategy.
